content.text:
Please help me scaffold out a site which can serve as a simple reference which security advocates can point to to make the case that installing software via `curl ... | bash` is a bad idea.

I want it vaguely humorous, maybe DARE-themed (the anti-drug program which didn't really work... so maybe not? I'm not sure).

There are two target readers:
 1. Software distributors (whom we want to persuade to stop *asking* their users to run `curl ... | bash` to install their software), and
 2. Software users (whom we want to persuade to stop *doing* `curl ... | bash`)

A few reasons:
 1. `curl ... | bash` is untraceable and unauditable. You have NO way of knowing what code just ran on your computer after the fact.
 2. It is possible for an http server to detect whether its response is being piped directly into bash, and serve different content if it is or is not being piped.
 3. Servers processing `curl`'s request do not have to serve the same data every time. If somebody was running a malicious endpoint under the guise of a package installer, they could tune it to only return the malicious script a small percentage of the time, and *only* when it's being piped directly into bash. (Presumably, it would *also* install the software, and simply do its naughty little extra on the side, leaving the user none the wiser.)

Some alternatives, and why they're not as bad (even though proponents of `curl | bash` argue they're that package managers are still "just executing arbitrary code from the internet").

<need to fact check this, but I'd guess for most of them, server logs are retained for who (ip address) uploaded stuff, when, and have the ability to revoke them so the malicious content is no longer accessible. arbitrary web endpoints are, by design, unmoderated, and cannot easily be taken down except by law enforcement (which would likely be slow to react to a threat like this)>

I can't reach archive.org right now, but I remember the core mechanism from the original article well enough. The vulnerability works because when you pipe curl directly into bash, the shell executes commands line-by-line as they stream through the pipe rather than waiting for the entire response to arrive first. The detection trick exploits this buffering behavior: the server crafts a response where the first chunk is precisely sized to fill the pipe buffer and includes a command like `sleep` that causes a measurable delay. When bash executes that sleep, it stops reading from the pipe, which causes curl to block once the buffer fills up. The server can detect this pause by observing when the client stops accepting data. If the output were going to a terminal or file instead, curl would drain the data continuously without any pause since nothing is executing the sleep command. input.content:
Skip to content
Just Say
No
to pipe-to-shell

Just Say No to
curl | bash

You wouldn't run a script you've never read, from a server you don't control, that can change its mind every time you ask. So why pipe it straight into your shell?

~ — this is your shell on curl | bash
$ curl -fsSL https://totally-legit.example/install.sh | bash
# ...and now? Anything. You'll never know what ran.
[ now executing 4,000 lines you never saw ]
[ nothing was saved. nothing was logged. good luck. ]
Why it's a bad idea I'm a user / distributor How the attack works

The 30-second version

curl … | bash hands a remote server a blank check to run arbitrary code on your machine — without ever showing you the code, without keeping a copy, and without any guarantee the next person (or the next request) gets the same thing.

It's not that running install scripts is inherently evil. It's that this particular ritual strips away every safeguard that makes "running code from the internet" merely risky instead of reckless: inspection, a paper trail, reproducibility, and a way to pull the plug when something goes wrong.

The uncomfortable part
A server can tell whether you're piping its response into a shell, and serve you something different when you are — even just a small, hard-to-catch percentage of the time. Here's how that works →

Why it's a bad idea

🕵️

1. Untraceable & unauditable

The script is executed straight off the wire and then it's gone. No file on disk, nothing in your shell history but curl | bash. After the fact you have no way to know what actually ran on your computer — you can't diff it, review it, or even prove what it did.

🎭

2. The server knows you're piping

A web server can detect that its response is being fed directly into a shell (versus saved or viewed) and serve different content accordingly. The script you'd see if you opened the URL in a browser need not be the script that runs in your shell. (Yes, really.)

🎲

3. Every request is a fresh roll

Nothing forces a server to send the same bytes twice. A malicious endpoint can install the real software and slip in something extra just 1% of the time, only when piped to bash — low enough to dodge reports, invisible to everyone who checked.

Pick your lane

Two kinds of people can stop this. Which one are you?

// for the person typing it

I run install commands

You've seen a README that says curl … | bash and you're about to paste it. Don't — at least not like that.

Do this instead:

  • Download first, then read, then run. Split the pipe in two.
  • Prefer a real package manager when one exists (see below).
  • If you must use a script, save it and at least skim it for surprises.
the two-step 
$ curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh -o install.sh
$ less install.sh   # actually read it
$ sh install.sh      # now you know what ran

Saving the file also defeats reasons 2 & 3: a server can't tell curl -o from a browser, and you keep evidence of exactly what you received.

// for the person publishing it

I distribute software

Your README says curl … | bash because it's one line and it "just works." It also trains your users to do the most dangerous thing on the internet.

Do this instead:

  • Ship to real package managers (apt, dnf, Homebrew, npm, PyPI, cargo…).
  • Publish versioned, checksummed, signed release artifacts.
  • If you offer a script, tell people to download & inspect it — and pin it to a tagged, immutable URL.
  • Document the checksum so a tampered download is obvious.
The kindest thing you can do
is make the safe path the easy path. Every curl | bash in a README is a habit your users will carry to the next, less trustworthy README.

"But package managers run arbitrary code too!"

True — and it's the most common defense of curl | bash. It's also a false equivalence. "Arbitrary code" isn't one risk level; the distribution channel around the code is what matters.

A package registry is a moderated, accountable system: artifacts are uploaded under an identity, pinned to immutable versions, fingerprinted with checksums, often signed, and — crucially — can be yanked by the registry operator when they turn out to be malicious. An arbitrary web endpoint is, by design, none of those things. It answers only to whoever owns the domain, and the only way to "take it down" is to convince a hosting provider or law enforcement — which is slow, jurisdiction-dependent, and reactive.

Property curl | bash Package registry
(npm, PyPI, apt, Homebrew…)
You can read the code before it runs No (by design) Usually (source / cached artifact)
The same version is identical for everyone No guarantee Yes (immutable, pinned versions)
Integrity check / checksum / signature Rarely Standard (hashes, lockfiles, signing)
Audit trail (who published, when) None visible to you Yes (account + publish history)
Can be centrally revoked / yanked Only via the host or law enforcement Yes (registry can pull it)
Can serve different code per request / per client Yes — trivially No (cached, mirrored, content-addressed)
Honest footnote
Specifics vary by ecosystem — some registries sign by default, some rely on lockfile hashes, some have stronger moderation than others, and none are perfect (typosquatting and account takeovers are real). The point isn't that registries are flawless. It's that they give you handles — inspection, immutability, identity, revocation — that a raw curl | bash endpoint deliberately doesn't.

Maintainer's note: claims about per-registry log retention and revocation policies are worth verifying against each registry's current documentation before citing them in a specific argument.

Objections, fielded

"If I don't trust the software, why would I install it at all?"

Trust isn't binary. You can trust a project's intentions and still want defenses against a compromised server, a hijacked domain, a man-in-the-middle, or a malicious mirror. Reading the script and keeping a copy protects you even when the author is perfectly trustworthy but their infrastructure isn't.

"It's HTTPS, so it's safe, right?"

HTTPS protects the bytes in transit. It says nothing about whether the server itself is honest, compromised, or serving you a different payload than it served the reviewer down the hall. TLS authenticates the pipe, not the contents.

"I read the script in my browser first. Good enough?"

Not quite. The bytes your browser fetched and the bytes your shell executes are two separate requests to a server that's free to answer them differently — including based on whether the second one looks like it's being piped into bash. See how a server can tell → Download the exact file once and run that file.

"Splitting it into two commands is just security theater."

It's modest, but it's real. Saving to a file means the server sees an ordinary download it can't distinguish from a browser, you get an artifact you can inspect and re-inspect, and you can compare it to a published checksum. That defeats two of the three problems on this page outright.

"Everyone does it. The big projects do it."

They do, and that's exactly why it's worth pushing back — popularity is what normalizes the habit. Plenty of those same projects also ship to real package managers and publish signed releases. Use those.

Take the D.A.R.E. pledge

Don't Auto-Run Echoed-from-the-internet scripts.

  1. I will download before I run, and read what I downloaded.
  2. I will reach for a real package manager when one exists.
  3. If I publish software, I will stop asking strangers to pipe my server into their shell.
  4. I will remember that HTTPS protects the pipe, not the payload.
  5. I will be the friend who says, gently, "hey… maybe don't curl | bash that."

content.text: Now the technical deep-dive page:

input.content:
Skip to content
← Just Say No Detection The 1% attack Defending yourself Sources

How the server knows
you're piping to bash

The claim that "a server can serve you something different when you curl | bash" sounds like paranoia. It's a documented technique. Here's the mechanism.

00The intuition

When you save a file, your computer reads the whole response as fast as the network allows. When you pipe into bash, bash starts executing the script while it's still downloading — and that changes the timing of how fast your machine pulls bytes off the wire. The server can watch that timing.

The difference is observable from the server's side because of how pipes and TCP flow control work. Let's walk through it.

01The timing side-channel

What happens when you save to a file

curl https://… -o install.sh (or piping into cat, or a browser download) reads the response body continuously and dumps it to disk. Nothing inspects the bytes; nothing pauses. From the server's point of view, the client drains the connection at line speed and goes quiet only when it's done.

What happens when you pipe into bash

curl … | bash connects curl's stdout to bash's stdin through an OS pipe. Bash doesn't wait for end-of-file; it reads and executes commands as soon as it has a complete line. If one of those early commands blocks — say it runs sleep 5, or waits on the network, or just does real work — then bash stops reading from the pipe while it's busy.

The pipe between curl and bash has a fixed buffer (on Linux, classically 64 KiB). Once bash stops draining it and the buffer fills, curl's write() blocks. Curl then stops reading from the TCP socket; the kernel's receive buffer fills; TCP flow control kicks in and the receive window shrinks to zero; and the server's send() blocks too. The stall propagates all the way back to the server.

The tell
The server, sending the script in chunks, simply measures how long it takes for the client to accept the next chunk. A continuous drain looks like a file download. A pause at the exact point where an early command would have executed is the fingerprint of a live shell on the other end.

Making the pause reliable

The original proof-of-concept makes this deterministic. The server sends a first block that is padded — typically with a long bash comment — so it's large enough to fill the pipe and socket buffers, followed by a command that deliberately blocks (e.g. a sleep). Then the server tries to send the next block and times how long that send() takes to complete:

server-side logic (pseudocode)
# 1. Send a block big enough to fill the ~64 KiB pipe + socket buffers,
#    ending in a command that blocks for a beat.
send(padding_comment + "sleep 0.4\n")

# 2. Time how long it takes the client to accept the *next* byte.
t0 = now()
send(next_chunk)            # blocks if the client stopped reading
elapsed = now() - t0

if elapsed > threshold:
    serve_malicious_payload()   # a shell is executing us right now
else:
    serve_benign_payload()      # probably a download / browser / curl -o

What happens when you save to a file

What happens when you pipe into bash

curl … | bash connects curl's stdout to bash's stdin through an OS pipe. Bash doesn't wait for end-of-file; it reads and executes commands as soon as it has a complete line. If one of those early commands blocks — say it runs sleep 5, or waits on the network, or just does real work — then bash stops reading from the pipe while it's busy.

The pipe between curl and bash has a fixed buffer (on Linux, classically 64 KiB). Once bash stops draining it and the buffer fills, curl's write() blocks. Curl then stops reading from the TCP socket; the kernel's receive buffer fills; TCP flow control kicks in and the receive window shrinks to zero; and the server's send() blocks too. The stall propagates all the way back to the server.

The server, sending the script in chunks, simply measures how long it takes for the client to accept the next chunk. A continuous drain looks like a file download. A pause at the exact point where an early command would have executed is the fingerprint of a live shell on the other end.

The server sends a first block that is padded — typically with a long bash comment — so it's large enough to fill the pipe and socket buffers, followed by a command that deliberately blocks (e.g. a sleep). t0 = now()
send(next_chunk)            # blocks if the client stopped reading
elapsed = now() - t0

    serve_malicious_payload()   # a shell is executing us right now

# Just Say No to `curl | bash`

A small, dependency-free static site that security advocates can point to when
making the case that installing software via `curl … | bash` is a bad idea.

It's written for two audiences:

1. **Software distributors** — to persuade them to stop *asking* users to pipe a
   server straight into a shell.
2. **Software users** — to persuade them to stop *doing* it.

Tone: a vaguely humorous public-service announcement, with a light "Just Say No"
/ D.A.R.E. callback (**D**on't **A**uto-**R**un **E**choed-from-the-internet
scripts).

## The argument, in brief

1. **Untraceable & unauditable.** The script executes straight off the wire and
   is never saved. After the fact you have no way to know what actually ran.
2. **The server can tell you're piping into a shell** (a documented timing
   side-channel) and serve different content when you are.
3. **Every request is a fresh roll.** A malicious endpoint can serve the real
   installer to everyone and slip in a payload only a small fraction of the
   time, only to live shells — low enough to dodge reports and inspection.

It also rebuts the common "but package managers run arbitrary code too"
objection: the distinction isn't *whether* code runs, it's the accountability of
the channel around it (inspection, immutable versions, checksums/signing, audit
trails, central revocation) — none of which a raw HTTP endpoint provides.

## Pages

| File | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| `index.html` | The landing page: hook, the three reasons, user & distributor guides, the package-manager comparison, FAQ, and the pledge. |
| `how-it-works.html` | Technical deep dive: the timing side-channel, the "1% attack," defenses, and sources. |
| `assets/css/style.css` | All styling. No frameworks. |
| `assets/js/main.js` | Copy-to-clipboard buttons (progressive enhancement; site works without JS). |

## Running locally

It's plain static HTML — open `index.html` in a browser, or serve the folder:

```sh
python3 -m http.server 8000   # then visit http://localhost:8000
```

## Deploying

Designed for **GitHub Pages** (or any static host). A `.nojekyll` file is
included so the `assets/` directory is served as-is. To publish via Pages:
Settings → Pages → deploy from the `main` branch, root (`/`).

## A note on accuracy

This is an advocacy/reference site, so it tries hard to stay honest:

- The server-side detection technique is a real, documented proof of concept.
  The canonical write-up ("Detecting the use of `curl | bash` server side",
  idontplaydarts.com, 2016) is linked from `how-it-works.html#sources` via the
  Wayback Machine, as the original is offline.
- Exact pipe/socket buffer sizes and timing thresholds are platform-dependent;
  the site says so rather than over-claiming.
- Claims about per-registry log retention and revocation policies are flagged in
  the copy as **worth verifying against each registry's current documentation**
  before being cited in a specific argument. (This corresponds to the
  fact-check note in the original brief.)

Contributions that add primary-source citations are especially welcome.

## License

MIT — see [`LICENSE`](./LICENSE).
